questions.q: What is the defining characteristic of a guardrail, as this lesson describes it?
options: It is enforced automatically at the moment an action happens, with no human in the loop deciding whether to allow it
It requires a human to explicitly approve each change before it proceeds
It only applies to production environments, never to development
It is slower than a gate by design
questions.explain: A guardrail — like an Azure Policy Deny or an AWS SCP — is a preventive, automated control with no approval step; it either allows the action or blocks it immediately.

questions.q: What is a gate, and why is it slower by design?
options: A gate is a type of automated policy check that runs faster than a guardrail
A gate is simply a guardrail with stricter rules but still no human involved
A gate only exists in AWS, never in Azure
A gate is a manual approval checkpoint where a human must look at a specific change and explicitly approve it, because the risk requires judgment that's hard to reduce to a rule
questions.explain: Gates exist specifically for risks that are genuinely novel or high-consequence and resistant to being fully encoded as an automated rule, which is why they require human judgment and therefore add latency.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what test should be applied before deciding a situation needs a gate?
options: Whether the team requesting it is new to the organization
Whether the concern could instead be rewritten as a guardrail — a rule a machine can check, like "don't do X without Y configured"
Whether the change costs more than the SCP enforcement budget
Whether a gate has ever been used for that resource type before
questions.explain: If the actual concern reduces to a checkable rule, it should become a guardrail (policy as code), not a manual gate — gates should be reserved for risk that genuinely resists being reduced to a rule.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as the risk of defaulting to gates for routine, everyday approvals?
options: Guardrails stop working once any gate exists in the organization
Gates automatically convert into guardrails after enough use
Teams start treating governance as an obstacle and route around it — provisioning resources manually outside the landing zone, the classic shadow-IT response
Cloud providers charge extra fees for organizations that use gates
questions.explain: When a sanctioned path like a change advisory board cycle is slower than the problem it's solving, teams tend to bypass it entirely, which is weaker governance than a well-designed guardrail.

questions.q: Why does a guardrail not cost time for a team whose change is actually compliant?
options: Because guardrails are optional and teams can choose to skip them
Because guardrails only run once per quarter during a scheduled audit
Because compliant changes are exempted from all policy checks
Because the check happens automatically at the moment of the action, so a compliant change simply proceeds without anyone noticing the guardrail is there
questions.explain: A guardrail's enforcement is automated and immediate — a team following the rules experiences no delay, which is the opposite of a gate's human review queue.
